top_choice_rationale: P001 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) best meets the common test of changing what can be credibly known, being validated by long use, and having attributable credit. The Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes framework estimates demand for differentiated products with endogenous prices and unobserved quality while keeping a structural link to theory. It made market power, substitution and merger effects measurable from market data. About three decades of use in merger review, antitrust, regulation, trade, health and environmental work has tested it, though I take that record from colleagues' statements and have not verified it. The three names map onto one jointly authored core if the citation stays on demand and competition in differentiated-product markets and does not claim the dynamic-industry strand. Caveats: it is a methods prize, BLP estimates are sensitive to instruments and functional form, and the three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. I rank P002 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn) second because its design-based evidence is strong but its persistence, magnitude and shift-share debates make it less mature. I rank P000 last because a mature, well-attributed candidate is available. The ten explicit supporters of P001 are not evidence of merit and I do not count them as such.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Autor, Hanson or Dorn. I have co-authored with committee colleagues Friberg, Boppart and Krusell, and I am an IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart. These are ties to members, not to candidates. Friberg works in industrial organisation and his arguments influenced my move to B005, so my agreement with him is not independent confirmation. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
